summary: A corm herb raises pale cups around dark central guides and nectaries after sustained soil wetting. Flowers open during sufficiently warm, calm dawns or later mornings, marking a temporary wet-season opportunity; summer dormancy leaves the meadow open.

links: Seasonal drought makes continuous foliage costly
A buried corm preserves reserves through dormancy
Sustained root-zone wetting permits emergence and flowering
chains.play: Read flowering patches as evidence of recent sustained wetting; harvest starchy corms at the cost of individual plants.
chains.weakness: Brief fog or surface dew cannot trigger a reliable bloom.

plausibility.judge: strict review: sol (codex) + DeepSeek; chair sol
plausibility.summary: Local moisture and developmental state govern flowering; blooms do not prove permanent or drinkable groundwater. Strict review (2026-11-19): Residual: F18 supplies a real summer drought pressure, and a buried reserve organ can support seasonal dormancy and emergence. Residual weakness: wetting alone does not demonstrate readiness to flower; sufficient stored reserves, suitable temperature and aerated soil are also necessary. The existing developmental-state qualification addresses this without requiring permanent groundwater.

analogues.mechanism: An underground corm stores reserves across seasonal shoot dormancy; the analogue concerns storage, not edibility.

chains.trait: Weather-dependent pale cups with scented nectaries and dark central guides
links: Long twilight provides a gradual light cue, but flowers open only when temperature and wind permit visitation (F3).
Cream petals contrast locally with green foliage once sufficient daylight reaches the patch; opaque fog limits distant visibility (F8).
Nectar-bearing tissue beneath the dark central guide emits a faint sweet scent that persists locally in still sheltered air (F16).
Shallow nectaries place feeding flies across low anthers and a central stigma, allowing pollen pickup and later deposition between flowers.
Visits may begin at warm calm dawns or shift into the morning; dark guides warm only when illuminated by useful sunlight.
chains.play: Watch weather-dependent fly visits and check for contact with anthers and stigmas; use open flowers as nearby landmarks.
chains.weakness: Cold, strong wind, rain and opaque fog delay opening or reduce visits; scent and pale petals do not guarantee pollination.
observe: Compare closed cups on a cold foggy dawn with open cups after the patch warms.
Watch a nectar-feeding fly brush anthers and the central stigma.
Find the faint scent at nectary tissue beneath the dark central guide.

plausibility.judge: strict review: sol (codex) + DeepSeek; chair sol
plausibility.summary: Fly pollination is inferred and must be observable. White petals reflect light; dark centres warm only under suitable sunlight. Strict review (2026-11-19): revised: Dawn activity and nectar discs were unsupported, so flowers now use scented nectaries, explicit reproductive contact and temperature- and wind-dependent opening. Still open: The dark-guide link is vacuous: a dark surface warms only when illuminated, so it cannot explain opening before useful sun, and the sentence restates its premise. No pollinator taxon is named, and the plant's core habitat is the east fog trap (F8, ~180 fog mornings/year), where fog blocks the 'sufficient daylight' cue and suppresses visitation. Cold dawn air also lowers volatile emission, so F16's still-air persistence does not by itself strengthen a dawn scent signal. The dawn specialization remains a just-so story.

analogues.mechanism: Open bowl flowers provide accessible nectar and reproductive surfaces; the scent source, dark guide and weather-dependent opening are proposed traits of this fictional species.

poison.signal: Green foliage and cream flowers with dark central guides identify this species; colour alone does not establish edibility.

gameplay.nest_material: Dry scapes and leaves in small quantities.
gameplay.notes: This species' sound corms are edible raw to player_lineage after removing soil and the fibrous outer tunic; no cooking is required. Corm removal kills that individual. Flowering indicates seasonal soil moisture, not permanent or potable groundwater.

relations.note: Excavates edible starchy corms and removes soil and the fibrous tunic before eating.
Hunts flower visitors; its own visits are not required for pollination.
Competes in seasonally moist open soil.

generator.trunk: None; slender scapes above buried 30–50 mm corms.

flower.nectaries: Shallow nectar-bearing tissue beneath the dark central guide emits a faint sweet scent.
flower.contact_geometry: Low anthers surround the feeding approach; a central stigma projects into the same fly contact path.
flower.opening: Require sufficient daylight, suitable temperature and low wind; opening may begin near dawn or wait until later morning.
flower.pollination: Show fly contact and pollen transfer when visits occur; poor weather can leave flowers unvisited.

overlay_rules: Six to nine cream petals surround a charcoal central guide around the nectaries.
Flowers 25–40 mm across; translucent, never luminous.
Dark guides may warm under direct sunlight; no warming benefit is assigned before useful illumination.

placement.fog: Humid dawns supplement seasonal rain but can delay warming and visitation.

generator.seasonal: Emergence requires sustained wetting and developmental readiness; daily flower opening follows suitable light, temperature and wind within the 26-hour day.
generator.wind_response: Scapes flex; strong wind suppresses opening and visits.

journal.en: The ground drinks first. Then its little candles open.
journal.es: Primero bebe la tierra. Después abre sus pequeñas velas.

secrets: Adjacent hollows can flower weeks apart when their soils retain water differently.
